design_detail: Phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial with an open-label crossover (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568), at one outpatient psychiatric clinic in San Anselmo, California, run from April 2015 to May 2018 (enrolment May 2015 to February 2017). Eighteen adults with moderate to severe anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (17 with cancer) were randomized about 1:3 to an inactive placebo (5) or MDMA (13) in two day-long experimental sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart, within manualized non-directive psychotherapy with a co-therapist pair (three preparatory and three integration sessions per experimental session). Primary outcome: change in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second experimental session, when the blind was broken; the MDMA group then had one open-label MDMA session and the placebo group crossed over to three, with follow-up 6 and 12 months after the last session (uncontrolled). Sponsored and fully funded by MAPS, organized by MAPS PBC.
can_establish: Whether, in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy were followed one month later by a larger fall in self-reported trait anxiety than the same psychotherapy with an inactive placebo, with a very imprecise estimate; which acute and next-week reactions were more frequent with MDMA in these 13 people.
cannot_establish: Whether there is a real difference (the 95% interval of the difference includes zero, with 5 people on placebo); how much of any difference reflects knowing one's allocation (86% of session guesses were correct) or the higher baseline anxiety of the MDMA group; whether benefits last (the 6- and 12-month data are uncontrolled after the crossover); rare harms; or effects in people with untapered psychiatric medicines, cardiovascular disease, brain tumours, ongoing first-line cancer treatment or a life expectancy under nine months, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Referrals from healthcare professionals, word of mouth and internet advertisements (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph); the registry adds printed advertisements. Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 110 preliminary telephone screens, 88 excluded for not meeting eligibility criteria or lost to contact, 22 in-person assessments, 1 excluded after the in-person screen, 21 enrolled, 3 discontinued after enrolment (1 unable to taper anxiolytic medicines, 1 unable to meet scheduling requirements, 1 deemed unfit by the investigator), 18 randomized. The main reasons for exclusion at telephone screening were living outside the study area and being too unwell to take part (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults aged 18 or older with a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness, ongoing or in remission with risk of recurrence, a life expectancy of at least nine months, anxiety primarily related to the illness on the SCID-I/P, and a STAI-Trait score of at least 45 of 80 (the text says 'scores … of 45'). Excluded: ongoing primary treatment such as initial chemotherapy; uncontrolled hypertension, significant cerebrovascular or cardiovascular disease, brain tumours, renal disease, dementing illness, type I or II diabetes, history of hyponatremia or hyperthermia, weight under 48 kg, pregnancy or lactation; psychotic disorders, bipolar I, dissociative identity disorder, eating disorders with active purging; inability to taper psychiatric medicines safely. Prescribed opioids were allowed, and people with substance use disorders in remission for at least 60 days could enrol (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Mean age 54.9 (SD 7.9); 14 women (77.8%); 15 White (83.3%); 17 with neoplasms and 1 with a musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder as the qualifying illness; histories of anxiety 83.3%, major depression 77.8%, PTSD 72.2%, insomnia 61.1%; prior ecstasy use 10 of 18 (55.6%), last use more than 10 years before in 6 of them; baseline STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) and STAI-State 57.4 (10.9) (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: All 18 were assessed at the primary endpoint and analysed by intention to treat (Fig. 1; Table 2 footnote). After the primary endpoint one MDMA participant stopped treatment because of cancer recurrence and died about a year later; 17 were followed at 6 and 12 months (Fig. 1; Table 3 footnote; Results, 6th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected, mostly White women with cancer living near one California clinic, well enough for day-long sessions and overnight stays, willing to stop psychiatric medicines and take MDMA; most had psychiatric histories and over half had used ecstasy before. Expectations of benefit were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded experimental sessions of about 8 hours, 2 to 4 weeks apart, with non-directive therapy by the same male–female co-therapist team, eyeshades and music, and an overnight stay with a night attendant; three 60- to 90-minute preparatory sessions before and integration sessions after each experimental session (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 1st to 4th paragraphs). MDMA was manufactured by David Nichols (Purdue University) and compounded with lactose placebo into capsules of identical appearance and weight (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph). The optional supplemental dose was taken in all but one session (Results, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth, 125 mg MDMA (or 125 mg lactose placebo) per session, with an optional supplemental 62.5 mg (or placebo) offered 1.5 to 2.5 hours later; two blinded sessions, then one open-label MDMA session (MDMA group) or three open-label MDMA sessions (placebo group) on the same schedule (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).
exposure.polysubstance: Psychiatric medicines had to be tapered. Seven of 18 (39.0%) took an opioid medicine during the study; six stopped it at least 3 days before and 2 days after each MDMA session, and one MDMA participant took tramadol but not within 24 hours of a session (Results, 1st paragraph). People with substance use disorders in remission for at least 60 days were eligible; drug screens were done before sessions (Methods › Study design and participants, 3rd paragraph; Procedures, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the primary outcome was assessed about one month after the second experimental session.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (125 mg lactose) with the identical psychotherapy (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized about 1:3 with a web-based system and numbered containers, monitored by staff who did not communicate with the site (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). With 5 and 13 people the groups differed at baseline: STAI-Trait 57.4 (5.2) vs 62.5 (7.3), STAI-State 51.8 vs 59.5, PTSD history 2 of 5 (40.0%) vs 11 of 13 (84.6%), anxiety history 60.0% vs 92.3%, insomnia 40.0% vs 69.2% (Table 1). The primary analysis compared change scores without adjustment for baseline (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; expectations of treatment were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Prior ecstasy use 3 of 5 on placebo vs 7 of 13 on MDMA (Table 1); opioid use not reported by group.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: STAI-Trait (20 items, 20 to 80), self-reported. Secondary: STAI-State; BDI-II; PSQI; Posttraumatic Growth Inventory (PTGI, with the illness as the reference event); MADRS and GAF, both by an independent blinded rater; FACIT-Sp (four subscales and additional concerns); Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ); Death Attitude Profile (DAP, five subscales); Self-Compassion Scale (SCS). Safety: spontaneously reported expected reactions during sessions and on seven daily telephone contacts afterwards, adverse events throughout, C-SSRS at each in-person visit and on two telephone days, vital signs every 30 minutes for 4 hours and hourly thereafter (Methods › Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Procedures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated instruments; STAI-Trait of 45 or more taken as moderate to severe anxiety (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: a larger fall in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second blinded session on MDMA than on placebo, by independent-samples t test of change scores; effect size Hedges' g (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Alpha 0.05 two-tailed for every test; the pooled t test or the Satterthwaite test chosen by a Folded F test of variances (Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph). Editors' count of 20 between-group tests at the primary endpoint in Table 2: STAI-Trait, STAI-State, BDI-II, PSQI, PTGI, MADRS, GAF, SCS, FFMQ, five DAP and five FACIT scores; plus 18 repeated-measures ANOVAs on the pooled follow-up data.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants, investigators and an independent rater were masked (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). The primary outcome is self-reported. At the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%) (Results, 8th paragraph). The MADRS and GAF were rated by an independent rater blind to group (Methods › Procedures, 4th paragraph); the rater's guesses were not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: STAI-Trait change −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo, P = 0.0558; Hedges' g 1.03, printed 95% CI −5.25 to 7.31 (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Abstract). Editors' calculations from the printed means and SDs: difference 14.7 points (95% CI −0.5 to 29.9; pooled t(16) = 2.06, P = 0.057); approximate 95% CI for g −0.05 to 2.12. Without the one placebo participant whose score fell by 35 points, P = 0.0066 (post hoc). Secondary at the primary endpoint (Table 2): PTGI +12.9 vs −2.6, P = 0.04, printed g 0.50; FFMQ +0.4 vs 0, P = 0.04, printed g 0.67; PSQI −3.6 vs −0.2, P = 0.05; STAI-State −22.1 vs −6.0, P = 0.10; BDI-II −20.9 vs −14.6, P = 0.36; MADRS −10.5 vs −7.0, P = 0.41; GAF +6.6 vs +3.0, P = 0.52; SCS, DAP and FACIT not significant. Editors' calculation for PTGI with the pooled SD: g about 0.73 (the printed P values for PTGI, FFMQ and PSQI match the unequal-variance test). Pooled uncontrolled follow-up (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months and 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months, F(3,48) = 51.39, P < 0.0001 (Table 3; Results, 4th paragraph).
analysis.covariates: None; change scores compared without adjustment for the baseline imbalance in STAI-Trait (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568: first submitted 13 April 2015, first posted 28 April 2015, before the actual start (14 May 2015). Registered primary outcome: change in STAI-Trait from baseline to the primary endpoint one month after the second experimental session, as reported; registered secondary outcomes match the measures in Table 2. Results posted 2 August 2021, with the same STAI-Trait values (−8.8 [14.7] and −23.5 [13.2]; endpoint 48.6 and 38.9). The record now names Resilient Pharmaceuticals as sponsor. The record's history of changes was not read (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The registered primary analysis is reported, but a post hoc analysis without one placebo participant (P = 0.0066) is presented in the Results, the Discussion and the Limitations as the likely reason for non-significance. Open-label session outcomes and adverse events are in the supplement (eTables), not read because the supplement is a Word download.
analysis.power: No power calculation: a feasibility study, sample size based on the phase 2 PTSD studies (Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph). With 5 controls the trial could detect only very large differences.

interpretation_gap.results_show: One month after two sessions, self-reported trait anxiety had fallen by 23.5 points on MDMA and 8.8 on placebo; the difference of 14.7 points has a 95% interval from about −0.5 to 30 (editors' calculation), so the trial cannot tell a large benefit from none. The MDMA group started 5 points more anxious, most participants and therapists could tell which pill had been given, and the primary outcome is self-reported. After everyone had MDMA, scores stayed lower at 6 and 12 months, with no control group. Jaw clenching, thirst, sweating, dry mouth and headache in sessions, and fatigue, extra sleep need and insomnia in the following week, were more frequent on MDMA; no serious adverse event was attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion attributes the non-significant primary result to one placebo participant with a large improvement, citing P = 0.0066 without that person, and to 2 placebo participants who believed they had MDMA (Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs), without weighing the much larger unblinding in the MDMA group or its higher baseline. It says the stable 6- and 12-month scores suggest the potential for benefits of up to a year or more, while acknowledging the lack of a control group (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), and that the durability "demonstrates benefits might extend beyond the acute treatment effects" (Discussion, 4th paragraph). It calls MDMA-assisted psychotherapy a safe treatment in this sample in which the benefits outweighed the costs (Discussion, 5th paragraph); the Conclusions call it possibly safe and feasible. The abstract reports the non-significant result (P = .056) with an effect-size interval that is impossible (Abstract).

timeline.event: This trial: the first randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for anxiety with a life-threatening illness (18 participants).
Barone et al., Front Psychiatry: a qualitative analysis of this trial's participants (on the project's evidence map; not read here).

replication.where_it_stands: One small pilot trial. The project's evidence map lists a registered trial in advanced-stage cancer (NCT00252174) that was terminated with results posted but no publication found, and a protocol for a double-blind trial in advanced cancer (EMMAC; Bhagavan et al., 2024); neither was read here. The Cochrane review covering psychedelic-assisted therapy in life-threatening disease (Schipper et al., 2024) is with the other reader of this batch.

funding.funder: MAPS, a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization, provided the MDMA and fully funded the study; MAPS PBC, its wholly owned subsidiary, organized the trial; MAPS and MAPS PBC assisted with study design, monitoring of study data, analysis, management and interpretation of data, preparation, review and approval of the manuscript and the decision to submit; the funder had no role in collecting data or conducting the study (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: P.W. received contractual support from MAPS as principal investigator; J.A., S.C. and E.S. were paid by MAPS as therapists in the study; E.W. was paid by MAPS as the independent rater; A.F., L.J., J.W. and A.E. were salaried full-time employees of MAPS PBC; B.Y.-K. and R.D. were salaried full-time employees of MAPS; S.H. received research funds from MAPS PBC as biostatistician; M.M. was paid as medical monitor (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Every author was paid by the sponsor in some role, including the independent rater, the therapists and the biostatistician responsible for the integrity of the data and analyses (Author contributions; Competing interests). The site is the principal investigator's own clinic (Center for Transformational Psychotherapy, San Anselmo; Author information). The paper's Crossref record carries no correction, expression of concern or retraction (read 2026-10-17).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered multi-site randomized trial in people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, comparing MDMA with an active comparator within the same psychotherapy, with baseline-adjusted analysis, independent raters, measured expectancy and blinding, and a controlled follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: Web-based randomization with numbered containers, managed by staff with no contact with the site; allocation concealed. The baseline imbalances (STAI-Trait 62.5 vs 57.4; PTSD history 84.6% vs 40.0%) are compatible with chance in 18 people, but because the analysis compares unadjusted change scores, the more anxious MDMA group had more room to improve.

Participants and therapists probably knew the allocation (correct guesses in 86.1% and 88.9% of sessions); the same co-therapy team delivered all sessions. Analysis by intention to treat, with no departures from the protocol reported up to the primary endpoint.
All 18 assessed at the primary endpoint.

The primary outcome is self-reported by participants who in most sessions correctly identified what they had received, in a trial whose volunteers were probably expecting benefit; knowledge of allocation could plausibly influence reported anxiety in both arms, in opposite directions. Expectancy was not measured.

Prospectively registered; the registered primary outcome and analysis are reported and agree with the posted results. The post hoc analysis excluding one placebo participant is extra, not a substitute, but it is given prominence; the 20 secondary tests are uncorrected (relevant to secondary results, not to this judgment).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-concealed randomized comparison, but the primary outcome is participant-reported in a trial where allocation was evident in most sessions, so the measurement domain is high and with it the overall judgment. The trial is also extremely small (5 controls), its primary difference is not statistically significant and its interval includes no difference. It can be cited for the observed change scores, for the frequency of acute and next-week reactions on MDMA in 13 people, and for the absence of serious adverse events attributed to MDMA; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for durability (the follow-up is uncontrolled) or for rare harms.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 110 telephone screens, 88 excluded at that stage, 22 assessed in person, 1 excluded, 21 enrolled, 3 discontinued before randomization, 18 randomized (5 placebo, 13 MDMA); all 18 completed the primary assessment; 5 and 12 completed the open-label stage and the 6- and 12-month follow-ups, 1 MDMA participant having stopped because of disease progression.
key_findings.note: The text says 92 of 110 failed telephone screening; Fig. 1 shows 88 excluded at telephone screening and 4 more before randomization (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Baseline, placebo vs MDMA: age 53.2 (10.5) vs 55.5 (7.0); women 4 of 5 vs 10 of 13; STAI-Trait 57.4 (5.2) vs 62.5 (7.3); STAI-State 51.8 (5.3) vs 59.5 (11.9); history of PTSD 2 (40.0%) vs 11 (84.6%), anxiety 3 (60.0%) vs 12 (92.3%), major depression 3 (60.0%) vs 11 (84.6%); prior ecstasy use 3 (60.0%) vs 7 (53.9%).

Primary outcome, STAI-Trait change from baseline to one month after the second blinded session: −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA (n = 13) vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo (n = 5), P = 0.0558; endpoint scores 38.9 (10.6) vs 48.6 (12.6); Hedges' g 1.03 with a printed 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9 (pooled t(16) = 2.06, P = 0.057); approximate 95% CI for g −0.05 to 2.12. The printed interval for g cannot be right (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Placebo change scores ranged from −1 to −35 (median −3, IQR 1.0); MDMA change scores from −43 to +1 (median −27, IQR 13.0). Excluding the one placebo participant with −35, the group difference would have been P = 0.0066 (a post hoc analysis).

Secondary outcomes at the primary endpoint, MDMA vs placebo change: PTGI +12.9 (23.2) vs −2.6 (6.1), P = 0.04, printed g 0.50; FFMQ +0.4 (0.6) vs 0 (0.2), P = 0.04, printed g 0.67; PSQI −3.6 (5.4) vs −0.2 (1.3), P = 0.05; STAI-State −22.1 (17.9) vs −6.0 (15.8), P = 0.10; BDI-II −20.9 (13.8) vs −14.6 (8.6), P = 0.36; MADRS −10.5 (8.2) vs −7.0 (7.2), P = 0.41; GAF +6.6 (9.7) vs +3.0 (12.5), P = 0.52; SCS P = 0.21; DAP and FACIT subscales P = 0.15 to 0.88.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with the pooled SD the PTGI g is about 0.73; the P values for PTGI, FFMQ and PSQI match the unequal-variance (Satterthwaite) test, which the Methods allow.

key_findings.finding: Uncontrolled follow-up of both groups after three MDMA sessions (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months, 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months, F(3,48) = 51.39, P < 0.0001; BDI-II 30.2 (10.8) to 3.0 (2.5), 3.2 (3.1) and 4.3 (4.0); MADRS 19.4 (7.5) to 4.1 (4.4), 3.6 (2.5) and 3.5 (3.2). Pairwise comparisons with baseline were not significant for any DAP subscale or for FACIT social/family well-being.

Expected reactions during the two blinded sessions, MDMA (n = 13) vs placebo (n = 5): jaw clenching 11 (84.6%) vs 1 (20.0%), thirst 11 (84.6%) vs 2 (40.0%), dry mouth 9 (69.2%) vs 1, perspiration 9 (69.2%) vs 0, headache 8 (61.5%) vs 1, lack of appetite 4 (30.8%) vs 0, anxiety 3 (23.1%) vs 0. In the following 7 days: fatigue 12 (92.3%) vs 3 (60.0%), needing more sleep 12 (92.3%) vs 2 (40.0%), insomnia 9 (69.2%) vs 2 (40.0%), low mood 8 (61.5%) vs 3 (60.0%), anxiety 8 (61.5%) vs 2 (40.0%), jaw clenching 8 (61.5%) vs 1; these decreased over the week.

Psychiatric adverse events from the first drug session to the day before session 3: anxiety, depressed mood, depression and dissociation in 1 MDMA participant each, insomnia 2 vs 1; no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour on the C-SSRS. Peak body temperature was the only vital sign that differed (37.3 [0.7] vs 36.9 [0.3] °C); no elevation needed medical intervention. One MDMA participant stopped after the primary endpoint because of cancer recurrence and died about a year later (five serious events related to the cancer and its treatment); two others had serious events from cancer progression during follow-up; none was attributed to MDMA.

Blinding: at the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%); three participants guessed wrongly at least once, two of them on placebo who guessed MDMA.

Registration and posted results: NCT02427568 first submitted 13 April 2015 and posted 28 April 2015, before the start on 14 May 2015; primary outcome change in STAI-Trait from baseline to the primary endpoint; results posted 2 August 2021 with the same STAI-Trait values; the adverse-event module lists 1 death and 3 participants with serious events in the MDMA group's 12-month follow-up period, all cancer-related terms (invasive ductal breast carcinoma, chordoma, spinal cord paralysis, meningitis, sepsis, cerebrovascular accident).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures; Results › Participant Flow, Outcome Measures, Adverse Events

key_findings.finding: Design rationale: the sample size was based on the phase 2 PTSD studies, with no power calculation; the Discussion cites, among the PTSD reports its safety findings agree with, the pooled phase 2 analysis (reference 53, Mithoefer et al., 2019), which PMC marks as retracted.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph; References, 53

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CI printed for Hedges' g (−5.25 to 7.31, in the abstract and the Results) is impossible for a standardized difference between groups of 13 and 5 with g = 1.03; the editors' approximate interval is −0.05 to 2.12, and the raw difference is 14.7 points (95% CI −0.5 to 29.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed interval cannot be cited; the correct interval still includes no effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say 92 of 110 screened people failed the inclusion criteria at telephone screening and then that three more were excluded after enrolment; Fig. 1 shows 88 excluded at telephone screening, 1 after the in-person screen and 3 after enrolment (92 not randomized in all).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite Fig. 1 for the flow.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of placebo participants who believed they had received MDMA is given as 2 of 5 (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and as '2 of 3 placebo participants' (Discussion, 6th paragraph); the Results say three participants guessed wrongly, two of whom were on placebo.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results, 8th paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs)
reporting_issues.consequence: Two of five placebo participants guessed MDMA at least once; the limitation paragraph misstates the denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the long-term reduction in anxiety was assessed by the MADRS, a depression scale; says there were significant gains in FACIT social and family well-being, although Table 3's comparisons with baseline give P = 0.72, 0.66 and 0.72; and says DAP fear of death, neutral acceptance and approach acceptance improved, although every pairwise comparison with baseline in Table 3 has P ≥ 0.10 (only the overall ANOVAs were significant).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are not supported by the paper's own tables.

reporting_issues.issue: For the PTGI the printed Hedges' g is 0.50, while the printed means and SDs give about 0.73 with the pooled SD (editors' calculation); the PTGI SD of the MDMA change is 23.3 in the text and 23.2 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; effect sizes for secondary outcomes should be recomputed rather than cited.

reporting_issues.issue: A post hoc analysis without one placebo participant (P = 0.0066) is presented three times as the likely reason the primary result was not significant; nothing in the Methods prespecifies outlier handling, and the participant's improvement is a valid observation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Methods › Statistical analyses)
reporting_issues.consequence: The prespecified result (P = 0.056, interval including no difference) is the one to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's participant flow shows all 13 MDMA participants completing the overall study, while Fig. 1 shows one who stopped after the primary endpoint because of disease progression.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the registry's period probably ends at the primary endpoint.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7686344 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4 as text, figure legends, the Fig. 1 CONSORT image viewed at its PMC address, funding, competing interests and contributions), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02427568 (API v2) for registration, outcomes, participant flow and adverse events; the Crossref record for the DOI. The supplementary Word file (eTables 1 to 6) was not read because it is a download; Fig. 2 values were not extracted.
